business models depend upon the type of technology and project size, that community shares are the cheapest and most commonly used form of finance for UK community energy projects and that the sector is currently financially successful, but its future viability is threatened by policy changes.

(1) business models of community energy projects depend on technology, scale, and the fine tuning to local contexts; (2) community energy is pioneering low cost citizen finance; (3) the sector is financially viable but needs policy support; and (4) the future of community energy is uncertain due to reductions in policy support and the lack of a long-term strategy.
community energy projects in England and Wales have pioneered the use of community shares as a financial mechanism for renewable energy projects.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the community energy sector has developed a variety of business models that have been adapted to local contexts and project sizes, but that it relies on a variety of financial mechanisms that are not always available or appropriate for new projects.
the business models and financial performance of community projects are diverse, and depend on the local context, but that the sector is vulnerable to policy uncertainty.

community energy projects are a promising alternative to the large scale energy provision but that they require a stable policy support and business models innovation in order to be sustainable in the longer term.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the business models and financing instruments that are used by the community energy sector are not only appropriate to the sector, but are also low cost and can be replicated elsewhere.
community energy has been able to develop low-cost financing solutions for renewable energy projects that can serve as a model for future low carbon investments.
the sector needs to innovate to find new business models that can deliver a surplus to communities, and that are resilient to policy changes.
